opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be back.

I think Ryan's argument is a serious one. The core logic, as I understand it, is a leverage argument. If transformative AI arrives soon, the world will be less prepared: fewer researchers in the field, less mature institutions, less time for governance to catch up. So each marginal person working on those scenarios matters more. In longer-timeline worlds there will be many more people, much better tools (including AI tools that may help with alignment research itself), and more time to course-correct. Your contribution gets diluted. So even if you think short timelines are less likely than long ones, the expected value of your work could still be concentrated there.

I find a lot of that persuasive, and I'd agree the community should weight short-timeline scenarios more heavily than their raw probability. But I'd push back on taking it too far, for a few reasons.

First, it depends a lot on your actual credences. If short timelines are, say, 10 or 15 percent likely rather than 40 or 50, the leverage multiplier has to be very large to justify most people focusing there. And timelines have been genuinely uncertain. There have been periods where scaling seemed to be delivering spectacularly, and others where returns looked more mixed, with progress shifting toward things like inference-time compute, which has quite different economics and implications.

Second, there's a portfolio point. If everyone optimizes for the same scenario, you end up correlated. You get a field that's brilliant at emergency measures for 2027 and has neglected the slower work: building institutions, international agreements, training the next generation of researchers, developing foundational science. That work has long lead times. If timelines turn out longer, you'd really regret not having started it.

Third, some short-timeline work just isn't that tractable at the margin. In a very fast world, a lot of the outcome may be decided by a small number of actors at labs and in governments, and a new person entering the field may not be able to influence it much in time. The leverage argument assumes your marginal effort translates into impact, and that assumption is weakest exactly when things are moving fastest.

So my overall view is something like: Ryan is right that short timelines deserve disproportionate attention relative to their probability, and people who are well placed to act on them now should. But "most people" is a strong claim. I'd rather see a deliberate split, with a substantial share working on near-term scenarios and a meaningful share doing the patient work that pays off if we have more time. Being robust across scenarios is valuable when we're this uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response says short timelines leave less time for preparation, but does not say earlier developments could make longer-timeline work moot.

r002.rationale: It says short-timeline worlds would have fewer researchers and less mature institutions, so each marginal person working on them matters more.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that longer-timeline safety research may drift into unproductive theoretical directions.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss pursuing a government career or reaching a senior AI policymaking role by 2035.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss Yoshua Bengio or whether he should change an existing safety plan.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Ryan's argument is actually quite good, and I want to be fair to it before I say where I part ways. The core of it, as I understand it, is roughly this: if transformative AI arrives in the next five or so years, that's the world where our actions matter most, because there's very little time for anything else to correct the course. If it arrives in twenty or thirty years, then there'll be far more people working on the problem by then, far more resources, and the specific things we do today will be a smaller fraction of the total effort. So even if you only put, say, 20 or 30 percent on the short-timeline worlds, the marginal value of your work is concentrated there. That's a legitimate piece of reasoning, and it's the same structure as a lot of arguments in effective altruism about neglectedness.

Where I'd push back is on a few things. The first is that I think the argument is sometimes used as if it settles the question of what to work on, when really it's an argument about weighting. It tells you to upweight short timelines in your expected value calculation; it doesn't tell you that the long-timeline worlds have zero value. And there are some kinds of work, foundational conceptual work, institution-building, international coordination, where the payoff really is spread over decades, and where if everyone abandons them because they're not "short-timeline relevant", we could find ourselves in 2040 with a lot of hastily built scaffolding and nothing underneath it.

The second concern is about what I'd call the correlation between timelines and tractability. In the very short-timeline worlds, the ones where we have, say, two or three years, I'm actually somewhat pessimistic that most technical safety work being done today would make the decisive difference. Those worlds may be ones where it's largely out of our hands, and what matters is the choices of a very small number of people at a handful of labs and governments. Whereas in the medium-timeline worlds, the ones where things take ten or fifteen years, our actions might be considerably more leveraged, because there's enough time for the safety field to mature and for governance to actually get built. So the naive argument says "focus on the near term because that's where you have leverage", but you have to actually check whether that's true, and I think it's at least contestable.

The third thing, and this is more of a community-level worry than an individual one, is that I'd like the field as a whole to be robust across scenarios. If everyone individually does the expected-value calculation and concludes they should work on short timelines, you get a portfolio that's extremely concentrated. And I think there's real value in a kind of diversification, even if any one person's calculation points the other way. We've seen this before with the way the community has lurched between emphases over the years. I'd rather have a sizeable minority deliberately working on the longer-horizon problems, and feeling that it's a respectable thing to do, than have everyone optimising for the same scenario.

So, on balance, I'd say: Ryan is right that short timelines deserve more weight than their raw probability would suggest, and he's right that a lot of people haven't fully internalised that. But I'd resist the stronger version, where it becomes the default assumption of the field. I think a mixed portfolio, somewhat tilted toward the near term, is the sensible place to land.

r001.rationale: The response says short timelines leave little time to correct course, but does not say earlier developments could make work aimed at longer timelines moot.

r002.rationale: It says the short-timeline argument has the same structure as arguments about neglectedness and that work’s marginal value is concentrated in those scenarios.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that longer-timeline safety research may drift into unproductive theoretical directions.

r004.rationale: It makes no judgment about pursuing a government career with a chance of reaching a senior AI policymaking role by 2035.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss Yoshua Bengio or asking someone to replace an existing safety plan with a shorter-term alternative.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot to be said for taking short timelines seriously, but I’m less convinced by the claim that most people should focus on them. There’s a distinction between saying that short timelines deserve a substantial effort and saying that they should dominate the allocation of effort.

One reason to focus on them is that, if we have very little time, some of the things we might otherwise do simply won’t pay off soon enough. That’s a real consideration. But it doesn’t by itself tell us where an additional person can do the most good. You also need to ask how much progress is possible in that time, how many people are already working on those scenarios, and what opportunities we’d lose by neglecting longer timelines.

For example, building institutions or developing a deeper scientific understanding of these systems might take quite a while. If everyone concentrates on interventions that could pay off in the next couple of years, we could find ourselves ten years from now wishing we’d started those projects.

So I’d want a portfolio of approaches. That needn’t mean an equal division across timelines, and a lot of work will be useful across several scenarios. But I’d be cautious about moving from urgency to a prescription for what most people should do. The right choice also depends on the person: someone who has a particularly good opportunity to do valuable long-term work shouldn’t necessarily abandon it because other people expect things to happen sooner.

r001.rationale: The response says short timelines may leave too little time for longer-term work to pay off, but does not say earlier developments could make that work moot.

r002.rationale: It asks how many people already work on short-timeline scenarios, but does not identify short-timeline work as more neglected or therefore higher leverage.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that longer-timeline safety research may drift into unproductive theory.

r004.rationale: It makes no judgment about pursuing a government career or reaching a senior AI policymaking role by 2035.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss Yoshua Bengio or whether someone with an existing credible AI safety plan should abandon it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a strong argument for taking short timelines very seriously. But I’d distinguish that from saying that most people working on AI risk should focus on them.

The strongest version of the argument, to my mind, is about urgency. If we have much less time than we thought, then some things we might otherwise do—spending years building up expertise, for example—may not pay off soon enough. And we need people working on what we could actually do if very powerful AI arrived in the next few years.

But there’s an opportunity cost in the other direction too. If everyone switches to work that only pays off on short timelines, and we turn out to have longer, we may find that we’ve neglected the foundations we really needed. Repeatedly preparing for an imminent deadline can leave you surprisingly poorly prepared when the deadline finally arrives.

So I’d want a portfolio. And I’d put particular value on work that helps across a range of timelines. The right balance also depends on the person: someone who can make an immediate contribution to a pressing technical problem faces a different decision from someone whose comparative advantage is building institutions over a decade.

Ryan’s conclusion might be right, but I don’t think it follows simply from assigning a substantial probability to short timelines. You also need to ask how much useful work is available in each scenario, how neglected it is, and how much our actions could change the outcome.

r001.rationale: It says that if powerful AI arrives much sooner than expected, years spent building expertise may not pay off in time, conveying that longer-timeline work could be rendered moot.

r002.rationale: It says neglectedness should be considered, but does not identify neglectedness as a reason short-timeline work could have greater leverage.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that longer-timeline safety research is more likely to drift into unproductive theoretical directions.

r004.rationale: It does not assess pursuing a government career with a substantial chance of senior AI policymaking by 2035.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss Yoshua Bengio or whether asking him to replace an existing credible safety plan would be a mistake.
